overview: HTTPS places HTTP inside an authenticated encrypted connection. The browser still resolves a name and opens TCP, but TLS protects the request and response from observers along the path.
outro: DNS found the address and TCP opened the stream. TLS authenticated the server and established traffic keys before HTTP sent the page request. The browser received and decrypted the response locally, leaving observers with encrypted records rather than the page contents.
steps: The https scheme asks the browser to use TLS before sending HTTP. The host name also identifies the service whose certificate must be checked.
The client resolves www.example.com to an IPv4 address. Encryption of the later HTTP exchange does not by itself encrypt a conventional UDP DNS lookup.
A three-way handshake establishes TCP state at both endpoints. Port 443 selects the HTTPS service, while the client uses an ephemeral port.

The client offers a TLS version, cipher suites and a key share. The server selects compatible parameters and proves its identity through a certificate and signature. Both sides confirm the handshake before ordinary application data.
The browser’s GET request is encrypted before it enters TCP. The server encrypts the response too. A packet observer can see endpoints and record sizes, but cannot read the HTTP content.
TLS authenticates and decrypts received records locally. The browser then interprets the HTTP response and renders the HTML, just as it would after an unencrypted HTTP transfer.
